findings.description: AWS access key ID and secret access key are embedded in plaintext in the EC2 user_data script, which is visible to anyone with instance metadata access or console/API describe permissions, leading to credential leakage.

The instance is deployed into a subnet with map_public_ip_on_launch enabled and attached to a security group allowing inbound SSH and HTTP from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing it directly to the internet with an increased attack surface, compounded by the leaked credentials in user data.
The EBS volume does not set encrypted = true, meaning data at rest on the volume is stored unencrypted, risking exposure of sensitive data if the underlying storage is compromised.
The EBS snapshot inherits the lack of encryption from its source volume, resulting in unencrypted snapshot data that could be shared or exposed without protection.

The security group allows inbound SSH (port 22) from 0.0.0.0/0, permitting any host on the internet to attempt authentication against the instance, significantly increasing the risk of brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks.

The security group allows inbound HTTP (port 80) from 0.0.0.0/0 with no compensating controls such as a WAF or load balancer, exposing the web service directly to untrusted networks over an unencrypted protocol.
map_public_ip_on_launch is set to true, causing any instance launched in this subnet to automatically receive a public IP address, expanding the internet-facing attack surface by default.

findings.issue_category: missing encryption and public access controls
findings.description: The S3 bucket storing VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration and no public access block or bucket policy restricting access, risking exposure or tampering of sensitive network traffic logs.
